explanation:
## The function

```cpp
bool clampTo(int& v, int lo, int hi)
{
    if (v < lo) { v = lo; return true; }
    if (v > hi) { v = hi; return true; }
    return false;
}
```

`int& v` is a **reference parameter**. `v` is not a new variable holding a copy
of the argument - it is another name for the caller's object. `v = lo` writes
through that name, so the caller's variable changes.

Everything else is passed by value: `lo` and `hi` are only read, so a copy of
each is exactly right, and copying an `int` is free.

## What changes when the `&` is missing

```cpp
bool clampTo(int v, int lo, int hi)      // by value
{
    if (v < lo) { v = lo; return true; } // modifies the parameter, nothing else
    ...
}
```

This compiles cleanly. It runs. It returns the right `bool`, so `changed 2` is
correct. And every value in the vector is unchanged, because `v` was a copy that
died when the function returned.

That is a genuinely instructive failure, because nothing about it looks wrong -
the only symptom is output that ignored the function entirely. If a function was
supposed to modify something and did not, the first thing to check is whether
its parameter is a reference.

Compilers do help here. With `-Wall -Wextra`, assigning to a by-value parameter
and never using it afterwards sometimes draws `-Wunused-but-set-parameter` -
sometimes, not always, because assigning to a parameter is perfectly legal and
occasionally intended.

## The same mistake one level up

```cpp
for (int& x : v)  if (clampTo(x, lo, hi)) ++changed;     // modifies v
for (int  x : v)  if (clampTo(x, lo, hi)) ++changed;     // modifies nothing
```

A range-for declares a variable that is initialised from each element in turn.
Without the `&` that variable is a **copy** of the element, so `clampTo` dutifully
modifies the copy through a perfectly good reference, and the vector never sees
it.

So the modification has to be by reference *all the way down*. One by-value link
anywhere in the chain silently breaks it, and the compiler cannot warn because
each individual step is legal.

The three forms worth knowing:

| Form | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `for (int x : v)` | a copy of each element; changes are discarded |
| `for (int& x : v)` | the element itself; changes stick |
| `for (const int& x : v)` | the element, read-only; no copy made |

For `int` the copy is free, so `const int&` buys nothing - but for a
`std::string` or a vector of vectors, `for (const auto& s : v)` avoids copying
every element just to look at it. That is the default to reach for.

## Why `<` and not `<=`

A value exactly equal to `lo` is already in range, so it is not changed and must
not be counted. `if (v <= lo) { v = lo; return true; }` assigns `lo` to a
variable that already holds `lo` - harmless - and then returns `true`, which
makes the count wrong.

The hidden case `1 100 1 100` within bounds `1 100` is there for exactly this:
all four values sit on a boundary, the correct answer is `changed 0`, and `<=`
reports 4.

## `lo == hi`

The range collapses to a single value, and the two tests still behave: anything
below becomes `lo`, anything above becomes `hi`, and they are the same number.
No special case needed - a sign the two independent comparisons are the right
structure rather than something cleverer.

## The separator

```cpp
bool first{ true };
for (int x : v)
{
    if (!first) std::cout << ' ';
    std::cout << x;
    first = false;
}
std::cout << "\n";
```

Printing `x << ' '` after each element leaves a trailing space, and printing
`' ' << x` before each leaves a leading one. The flag puts the separator
*between* elements, which is what "separated by spaces" means, and it handles
the empty list by printing nothing at all.

`std::cout << '\n'` rather than `std::endl` throughout, by the way. `std::endl`
writes a newline *and flushes the stream*, which for output written in a loop
means a system call per line. For a program whose output is a few lines it does
not matter; the habit matters, because the same code in a loop over a million
lines is a hundred times slower for no benefit.

## What C++ already has

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
x = std::clamp(x, lo, hi);
```

`std::clamp` since C++17 returns the clamped value rather than modifying in
place, which composes better and is what you would use in real code. It cannot
tell you whether it changed anything, which is why this exercise asks for the
reference version - and the counting is the part that makes the reference
earn its place.
